lesson.title: Random assignment

lead.text: Start with the gym's own comparison. Members were free to join the programme or stay out, and the manager compared the two groups three months later. The trouble is that the groups differed long before the programme began. Someone who volunteers for a fitness programme is likely to be someone who already exercises, enjoys it and has the time.

So the joiners may have been fitter on the first day, and the gap three months on may come from that head start. When people sort themselves into groups on a trait that bears on the result, the effect is called self-selection. Here the trait is how much people already exercise, and it works as a confound built into the design, much as the weather did in the seaside town.
The next screen puts numbers on how large such a head start can be.
Eight members can choose. Four who exercise a lot choose the new programme, and the other four mostly stay away.

The repair is to take the choice away from the members. Write each name on a slip of paper, shuffle the slips and draw them. The first half go into the programme, and the rest form the control group, who carry on as before and give something to compare against. The draw does not care whether a member is keen or lazy, fit or unfit.

This is random assignment: every person has the same chance of landing in either group. The figure shows one set of twelve members, each with a score for how fit they were before the study, divided up three different ways by chance.

afterFigure.text: No draw makes the groups identical, and the three here differ by different amounts. What the draw guarantees is that no trait favours one group. A member who is fit, keen or short of time is as likely to be in one group as the other. That holds for traits nobody thought to measure, which is something no amount of careful choosing by researchers could promise.

lead.text: Random assignment makes the groups fair, which is a weaker thing than making them equal. Suppose the draw puts people with fitness scores 5, 9, 4 and 6 in group A, and people with scores 7, 3, 8 and 10 in group B. Group A adds up to 24, and 24 divided by 4 gives an average of 6. Group B adds up to 28, which gives an average of 7.

Group B starts one point ahead, and nothing has yet been done to either group. That gap is chance. Draw again and the gap changes, and sometimes group A will be the one in front. What matters is that the draw never leans one way: over many draws the gaps cancel out, and in larger groups each gap tends to be smaller.
A small study can still be unlucky. The remedy is more people in the groups, and the draw itself stays.
Two groups were drawn at random. Group B started with an average one point above group A, before anything was done to either group.

steps.headline: What you set and what you measure

lead.text: With fair groups in place, the gym still has to say exactly what it is comparing. In the study the researchers decide one thing: who gets the programme. That is the independent variable. Afterwards they measure an outcome to see whether it changed, such as each person's resting heart rate after three months. The measured outcome is the dependent variable, because its value depends on the condition.

The outcome also needs a precise meaning. Fitness is a loose word, and one researcher may take it to mean strength while another means stamina. An operational definition says exactly how a concept will be measured, such as the distance a person covers in a 12-minute run. Anyone could repeat that measurement and get comparable numbers.
Fixing these choices before the data arrive stops researchers from searching afterwards for some outcome that happens to differ.
Researchers assign people at random to a fitness programme or no programme. After three months they measure each person's resting heart rate.

Random groups and clear measures still leave one problem. People often improve simply because they expect to, and symptoms often fade with time anyway. If one group takes a drug and the other takes nothing, the drug group improves for three reasons mixed together: the drug, the expectation and the passing time.

The fix is to give the control group an identical-looking pill with no active ingredient, called a placebo. Now both groups expect to be treated and the same time has passed. The placebo group shows how much improvement expectation and time produce on their own, so only the extra improvement in the drug group can be credited to the drug.

Expectation can leak in a second way. If the people who measure the symptoms know who received the drug, their judgement can lean towards the result they hope for, often without their noticing. And if participants can tell which pill they were given, the placebo no longer keeps their expectations equal.

A double-blind trial closes both gaps. Neither the participants nor the people measuring them know who received the drug until the results are in. If only one of the two parties is kept in the dark, the trial is single-blind. Together with random assignment and a placebo, double-blinding leaves the treatment as the one difference between the groups.
The control group in a drug trial gets a pill that looks the same as the real one but has no active ingredient.
A drug trial gives one group the drug and another an identical-looking placebo. Both groups improve on a symptom score.

lesson.orientation: See why only random assignment to conditions lets an experiment rule out confounds.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A gym lets its members choose whether to join its new fitness programme. Three months later the manager tests everyone and finds that the joiners are fitter than the members who stayed out. A friend says that proves the programme works, and the manager would like to put the figures on a poster.

The last lesson showed how a pattern can come from something hiding behind it, and the gym's comparison has that problem. The groups were not made fairly, and the result may say more about who joined than about what the programme did.

This lesson builds the test the gym should have run. We take the version it ran and repair it one flaw at a time. Each repair closes off a way for the result to mislead, until the only difference left between the groups is the programme itself.

intro.promise: By the end you'll explain why random assignment makes a fair comparison, and name the variables, placebo and blinding a fair trial needs.

recap.keyIdea: Random assignment gives everyone an equal chance of each condition, so no trait systematically favours one group. A placebo and blinding keep expectation equal, and the gap that remains is the treatment.

blocks.text: Back at the gym, you can now say why the manager's comparison could not be trusted. You found that volunteers began 6 hours a week of exercise ahead, and that a chance gap of 0.5 is no sign of bias. You also found that a drug's own effect is 12 − 8 = 4 points once the placebo response is taken away.

recap.nextHook: A fair trial can show that a programme made a difference, but not whether the difference is big enough to matter, and the next lesson begins with a training course that raised scores by 6 points in two very different classes.

questions.prompt: A random draw puts people with prior fitness scores 4, 6, 5 and 7 in the treatment group, and 6, 5, 4 and 5 in the control group. What is the treatment mean minus the control mean?
hints: Find the mean of each group of four.
Subtract the control mean from the treatment mean.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Treatment mean = 22/4 = 5.5; control mean = 20/4 = 5; the chance gap is 0.5.

questions.onCorrect: Each mean is its total divided by four. The chance gap is small, as random assignment leads you to expect.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the treatment group's own mean. Subtract the control group's mean from it.
Check the order. The question asks for the treatment mean minus the control mean.

questions.prompt: In a trial, neither the participants nor the researchers who measure them know who received the real treatment. What is this design called?
hints: Count how many parties are kept unaware.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a double-blind design: both sides are kept unaware of the conditions.

questions.onCorrect: Both sides are kept unaware of the conditions, so neither expectation nor measuring can lean toward the treatment.

misconceptions.feedback: A single-blind design keeps only one party unaware. Count how many parties are unaware here.

questions.prompt: A researcher records 'aggression' as the number of seconds a participant holds down a button that blasts noise at an opponent. What do we call a definition that turns a concept into a precise measurement like this?
hints: The definition tells you the operation used to measure the concept.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is an operational definition: it states exactly how aggression will be measured.

questions.onCorrect: An operational definition says exactly how a concept is measured, so anyone could repeat the measurement.

misconceptions.feedback: Those name the variable set and the variable measured. This asks what turns a concept into a measurement.

questions.prompt: What is the best reply to the friend?
hints: Think about who is likely to sign up for a fitness programme.
Were the two groups equally fit before the programme began?

acceptedIdeas: Not necessarily: fitter members may have been the ones who chose to join.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not necessarily: fitter members may have been the ones who chose to join.

choices.label: Yes: if joiners are fitter, the programme has worked.
Only if the joiners lost weight.
Not necessarily: fitter members may have been the ones who chose to join.

questions.onCorrect: People who choose a programme differ from those who do not. You spotted that before anyone gave it a name.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the final gap as the programme's work. Ask who chose to join in the first place.
Weight is one possible outcome, but it does not fix who chose to join.

questions.prompt: Random assignment gives every participant an equal what of being placed in each condition? Answer in one word.
hints: Think of a coin toss deciding each person's group.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An equal chance: assignment depends on the draw, never on the person.

questions.onCorrect: Assignment depends on the draw, never on the person, so no trait can decide who gets the programme.

misconceptions.feedback: Choosing is self-selection. Random assignment takes the choice away.

questions.prompt: Four members who choose the programme exercise 9, 8, 8 and 7 hours a week. The other four exercise 3, 2, 2 and 1. How many hours a week higher is the programme group's average, before the programme starts?
hints: Add the four values in a group and divide by four.
Subtract the comparison group's mean from the programme group's mean.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Programme mean = (9 + 8 + 8 + 7)/4 = 8; other mean = (3 + 2 + 2 + 1)/4 = 2; the head start is 6 hours.

questions.onCorrect: Each group's average is its total divided by four. The joiners' head start is built in by choice.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the programme group's own average. The question asks how far ahead it is of the other group.
That compares totals, and both groups have four people. Compare the averages instead.

questions.prompt: Why is a one-point gap before the study no problem for random assignment?
hints: Does one draw guarantee equal groups, or only fairness?

acceptedIdeas: It promises no trait systematically favours one group, not that the groups are identical.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Random assignment promises fairness, not equality in one small study.

choices.label: Because random assignment makes the groups exactly identical.
It promises no trait systematically favours one group, not that the groups are identical.
Because the treatment will cancel the gap.

questions.onCorrect: Chance gaps are expected in a small study. Random assignment only ensures no trait leans one way.

misconceptions.feedback: One draw of eight people cannot make groups identical. The gap just seen proves that.
The treatment has not been given yet. The gap exists before it.

questions.prompt: Which is the best operational definition of “fitness”?
hints: An operational definition states exactly what will be measured.

acceptedIdeas: The distance a person covers in a 12-minute run
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The distance covered in a 12-minute run is a precise measurement anyone could repeat.

choices.label: How athletic a person looks to the researcher
How fit a person says they feel
The distance a person covers in a 12-minute run

questions.onCorrect: A good operational definition is a measurement someone else could repeat exactly.

misconceptions.feedback: That depends on opinion, so two researchers could disagree. Choose a measurement.
That relies on a feeling, not a measurement anyone could repeat.

questions.prompt: Is resting heart rate the independent or the dependent variable?
hints: Ask which variable the researchers set and which they measure.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Resting heart rate is the dependent variable: it is measured to see the programme's effect.

questions.onCorrect: Resting heart rate is measured afterwards to see the programme's effect, so it depends on the condition.

misconceptions.feedback: The independent variable is the one the researchers set. Resting heart rate is measured after the condition is set.

questions.prompt: Why give the control group an identical-looking pill with no active ingredient?
hints: What else, besides the drug, might make people improve?

acceptedIdeas: So that expectation is the same in both groups
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It keeps expectation equal, so only the active ingredient differs between the groups.

choices.label: So that expectation is the same in both groups
So that the control group cannot improve
So that the drug group takes longer to improve

questions.onCorrect: Equal pills mean equal expectation. Only the active ingredient then differs between groups.

misconceptions.feedback: The control group can still improve through expectation and time. That is the point of the pill.
The pill is about what people expect, not how long they take.

questions.prompt: In a drug trial the drug group improves by 12 points and the placebo group by 8 points. How many points of improvement can be attributed to the drug's active ingredient?
hints: The placebo group improves without any active ingredient.
Remove the improvement that both groups share.
Subtract the placebo improvement from the drug improvement.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 − 8 = 4 points. The placebo group shows how much improvement expectation and time alone produce.

questions.onCorrect: Remove what both groups share. The placebo group shows what expectation and time produce alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the drug group's whole improvement, including what expectation alone produces.
That is the improvement without the active ingredient. Ask what the drug added beyond it.
Adding the groups mixes the two responses together. You need what is left after removing the shared part.
